extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, regulators, and legal academics
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and normative evaluation of public participation in administrative rulemaking, focusing on who comments, the content and sophistication of comments, agency responsiveness, and institutional design alternatives to improve regulatory democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who participates (demand-driven participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under existing law, agencies writing regulatory rules receive input only from those who decide they have sufficient resources and interest to send them — such as organized interest groups or companies facing compliance costs under the new rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate the representativeness of comment pools and to assess whether participation is skewed toward organized interests and regulated entities; highlights the role of resource and interest constraints in shaping participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical supposition: technical/scientific expertise suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that regulatory problems can be resolved through the application of technical, scientific expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a justificatory premise for limiting broad public participation; the article questions this assumption empirically and suggests it should be evaluated against evidence about what types of knowledge and perspectives are actually relevant to rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical supposition: public lacks interest in participating
rubrics_metrics.description: The supposition that individual members of the public tend to lack interest in participating in regulatory policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify minimal outreach or reliance on organized interests; the article tests this claim by measuring the presence and proportion of lay public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical supposition: laypersons add little value
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that even if individuals had interest, they would add little to a process already informed by the views of organized interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as a normative defense of the status quo; the paper examines whether lay comments raise relevant concerns and whether they add perspectives not covered by interest groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of lay-public comments (public demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments from the lay public make up a substantial proportion of total comments about some regulations, indicating potential public demand for participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative metric for detecting latent public demand; can be used to challenge claims that the public is uninterested and to argue for broader engagement mechanisms when lay participation is substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic differences exist in the sophistication of comments from interest groups versus individual members of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the technical quality, evidentiary support, and policy sophistication of submissions; informs whether capacity-building or institutional design changes are needed to raise lay sophistication or to weigh different types of input appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to agency's legal mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: Laypeople nearly always raise concerns that are relevant to the agency’s legal mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether non-expert comments contribute legally cognizable or policy-relevant points; counters the claim that lay input is irrelevant by showing relevance even when sophistication differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency acceptance / responsiveness to suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophistication affects the agency’s acceptance of suggestions in public comments even when controlling for differences in the person or organization making a comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures how agency decisionmaking responds to comment content and quality rather than simply commenter identity; implies that improving comment sophistication or structuring input could change agency uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth/diversity of concerns raised
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups do not always raise the range of concerns raised by comments from the lay public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates whether organized interests capture the full spectrum of public concerns; highlights the unique contributions of lay commenters in surfacing diverse perspectives that organized actors may overlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process effects on public interest and sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger public’s interest in a particular regulation, and its sophistication to take part in discussing it, are both themselves shaped by the process of how the public is consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats consultation design as endogenous — the method and timing of outreach affect who participates and how informed they are; implies that procedural reform can increase both interest and comment quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and knowledge-expanding potential of alternative institutional designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative institutional designs are feasible, and they would provide regulators with valuable expanded knowledge about how informed members of the public react to regulatory rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating reform proposals: practicality of implementation and the potential to produce actionable, expanded knowledge for agencies; supports experimentation with designs that solicit more informed lay input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative defenses: representative politics or political infeasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A principled defense of the current approach would rest most plausibly either on an idealized conception of representative politics and interest group politics, or on a sense that no changes to regulatory democracy are politically feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate the normative legitimacy of the status quo by requiring proponents to justify reliance on existing processes either theoretically (representative politics) or pragmatically (political feasibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints: limited public attention to complex issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Real world constraints such as limited public attention to complicated regulatory issues are invoked to accept current compromise approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as a practical constraint to weigh against democratic ideals; can be empirically tested (e.g., by measuring attention and engagement) and used to judge whether process improvements can realistically increase meaningful participation.
